newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN blasts Malaysian ruling as dangerous precedent.
newsitem.headline: UN blasts Malaysian ruling as dangerous precedent.

text.p: A senior United Nations official on Tuesday accused a Malaysian court of undermining the authority of the U.N. human rights system by allowing a libel suit to go ahead against a lawyer working for the world body, rejecting his claim of immunity from legal action.

Ralph Zacklin, acting U.N. Commissioner for Human Rights, issued a firm statement in Geneva expressing concern over the court ruling on Saturday in the case brought in December by two Malaysian companies against Param Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian lawyer working for the U.N. as an expert.

He said the ruling set a "dangerous precedent" by usurping the authority of U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan. Cumaraswamy serves as the U.N. special rapporteur (investigator) on the Independence of Judges and Lawyers.

The two firms, MBf Capital Bhd and MBf Northern Securities Sdn Bhd, claimed that Param had defamed them in an article published in the November 1995 issue of the International Commercial Litigation magazine, a London-based publication. In the article, Param was quoted as saying he was investigating complaints that businessmen were manipulating the Malaysian judicial system.
But Judicial Commissioner Zainun Ali on Saturday dismissed Param's request to strike out the 60 million ringgit ($23.8 million) suit and gave Param 14 days to file his defence.
Zacklin, who is standing in until Irish President Mary Robinson takes over the top rights post, is expected to discuss the case with Annan, who arrives on Wednesday in Geneva.
The Geneva-based Centre for the Independence of Judges and Lawyers has called on Annan to immediately bring the case of Param's immunity before the International Court of Justice.

"In its decision, the Court held that the certificate given by the Secretary-General of the United Nations confirming the Special Rapporteur's immunity from legal process was merely an opinion which is not binding upon the court," Zacklin said.

"This decision establishes a dangerous precedent by undermining the immunity accorded to an expert who is on mission for the United Nations," added the British lawyer, whose regular job is director of the office of the U.N. legal adviser.

"In deciding that a national court has the jurisdiction to determine whether a Special Rapporteur is acting in the course of the performance of his mission, the court is usurping the exclusive authority of the Secretary General to determine whether the words spoken or written or acts done by experts on mission are performed in the course of their mission, and therefore, entitled to immunity from legal process of every kind," he said.

If allowed to stand, the decision presents a "serious threat" to the special procedure mechanisms of the U.N. Commission on Human Rights, a "pillar of the United Nations human rights programme", according to Zacklin.

"If independent experts and special rapporteurs are denied such immunity and subjected to legal process in domestic courts, this would have a negative effect on their ability to carry out their mandates and to report on violations of human rights, thus undermining their independence," he concluded.

U.N. legal officials in New York called in Malaysian diplomats on Monday to express concern that the ruling meant Kuala Lumpur was not fully complying with a 1946 U.N. convention on privileges and immunities, U.N. sources in Geneva said.

"This is a serious threat to all special rapporteurs -- if the precedent is allowed to stand, any special rapporteur who offends private individuals or government officials could be sued," a U.N. source said. "It could never end."

The U.N. Centre for Human Rights has 13 special rapporteurs to look into abuses in specific countries -- including Burma, Iran, Iraq and Nigeria -- and 11 thematic investigators who examine abuses worldwide including executions and torture.
